UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                          BEFORE THE
             FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION



PJM INTERCONNECTION, L.L.C.          DOCKET NOS. EL25-49-000
                                                 EL25-49-001




REPLY PROTEST OF THE MARYLAND OFFICE OF PEOPLE’S COUNSEL ON
           PJM’S PROPOSED TERMS AND CONDITIONS

                               DAVID S. LAPP
                               PEOPLE’S COUNSEL

                               William F. Fields
                               Deputy People’s Counsel

                               Philip L. Sussler
                               Senior Assistant People’s Counsel

                               Mark S. Byrd
April 24, 2026                 Assistant People’s Counsel
        Pursuant to the Commission’s December 18, 2025 order setting an April 17, 2026

deadline for replies,1 which was extended one week by notice issued January 23, 2026,

the Maryland Office of People’s Counsel (“MPC”) respectfully submits the following

reply regarding PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) initial brief (hereinafter, “PJM

Initial Brief”) and responsive pleadings submitted in the above captioned proceeding.



                                       INTRODUCTION

       PJM’s co-location proposals in this docket have major implications for Maryland’s

residential ratepayers due to the potential impact on capacity market prices. The impact

on existing customers depends on whether and how co-located arrangements between

new large loads and existing generation effects supply in the Base Residual Auction

(“BRA”) or effects procurement targets in PJM’s planned reliability backstop

procurement (“RBP”). This distinction is substantial considering the BRA will allocate

costs across the system, whereas the RBP, as currently under consideration in the PJM

stakeholder process, may allocate costs to individual electric distribution companies

(“EDCs”) and/or load serving entities (“LSEs”) on a pro rata or other basis.2 As described

by PJM’s Independent Market Monitor, co-locating data center loads with existing

 generation reduces the supply of capacity to the BRA, thereby increasing capacity

prices.3

        Additionally, PJM’s co-location proposals with respect to existing generation are

inconsistent between this docket and the compliance filing in Docket No. ER26-1479-

000. Whereas PJM’s compliance filing in Docket No. ER26-1479-000 proposes tariff

revisions that would facilitate new large loads co-locating with existing generators, PJM’s

filing in this docket suggests that only new generation is eligible for the new transmission

services.4 These inconsistencies render it impossible to determine the effect of these

proposals on ratepayers. The Commission should therefore require PJM to clarify

whether these co-location rules are intended to apply to co-location arrangements

undertaken with existing baseload generation so the effect of these transmission services

on ratepayers can be determined and, if so, how adverse impacts on existing (particularly

residential) customers can be mitigated.

        The Commission should not accept co-location rules that facilitate the

interconnection of large load data centers to the detriment of residential ratepayers. Such

an outcome would be at direct odds with the statement of principles signed by the

National Energy Dominance Council within the White House and thirteen governors of

intended to serve Co-Located Load will be constructed and operational before June 1, 2029).


                                                   2
 states within PJM5 stating that PJM’s tariff revisions should reflect how costs are

allocated to data centers to protect residential customers. It would also contradict the

White House’s ratepayer protection pledge that companies will build, bring, or buy the

new generation resources and electricity needed to satisfy their new energy demands,

paying the full cost of those resources whether by building, or buying from, new or

otherwise additive power plants.6


                                        BACKGROUND

    1. Show Cause Order:

       On December 18, 2025, the Commission determined that PJM’s tariff is unjust and

unreasonable, explaining generally that the tariff:

       does not contain provisions addressing with sufficient clarity or consistency
       the rates, terms, and conditions of service that apply to Interconnection
       Customers serving Co-Located Load, including generators serving Co-
       Located Load in a configuration with special protection schemes to prevent
       the Co-Located Load from taking energy from the transmission system.7

The Commission directed PJM to revise its tariff to provide clarity regarding the

responsibilities of existing interconnection customers seeking to serve co-located load

using their generating facilities.8 The Commission also directed PJM to file tariff changes

specifying that an interconnection customer seeking to serve co-located load using an

 existing generating facility must bear the costs of all network upgrades that PJM finds are

necessary to preserve transmission system reliability for existing transmission

customers.9

        Furthermore, the Show Cause Order also required that PJM define “Co-Located

Load” as a “configuration [that] refers to end-use customer load that is physically

connected to the facilities of an existing or planned Customer Facility on the

Interconnection Customer’s side of the Point of Interconnection to the PJM Transmission

System.”10 The Commission clarified that an existing generating facility may not begin

serving Co-Located Load that is not Network Load until it has delisted its Capacity

Interconnection Rights for the portion of the generating facility to be designated to serve

any Co-Located Load that is not receiving network integration transmission service

(“NITS”).11

        The Commission’s Show Cause Order in this proceeding also directed PJM to

revise its tariff to allow eligible customers seeking to take NITS on behalf of co-located

load to take a new interim, non-firm transmission service until all Network Upgrades

necessary to provide NITS are complete. The Commission also directed PJM to offer two

other new transmission services—a firm contract demand transmission service and a non-

firm contract demand transmission service—that an eligible customer can choose to take

on behalf of a co-located load instead of taking NITS.”12

      2. White House and PJM Governors Statement of Principles and White House
        Pledge

        On January 15, 2026, the National Energy Dominance Council within the White

House and thirteen governors of states within PJM signed the Statement of Principles

urging PJM to expeditiously file proposed tariff revisions with the Commission that

reflect a set of principles for how generation capacity for data centers should be procured,

and how costs should be allocated to data centers to protect residential customers.13

Specifically, under these principles, PJM should hold a procurement for capacity through

the conduct of at least one reliability backstop auction (“RBA”) to procure new capacity

resources, with the costs of such new capacity going primarily to load serving entities

with new data centers that have not self-procured new capacity or agreed to be

curtailable.14

        On March 4, 2026, the White House issued the Ratepayer Protection Pledge that

companies will build, bring, or buy the new generation resources and electricity needed

to satisfy their new energy demands, paying the full cost of those resources whether by

building, or buying from new or otherwise additive power plants.15 The pledge also

provides that where possible, these companies will also add more capacity that serves the

broader public by increasing supply.16

      3. PJM Board Letter

        On January 16, 2026, the PJM Board of Managers (“Board”) issued a decisional

letter expressing that PJM’s system is at higher risk than ever due to the PJM’s capacity

market clearing short of its reliability requirement for the first time in history in the

2027/2028 BRA.17 The Board determined that this outcome is unacceptable and warrants

corrective action through initiation of a reliability backstop procurement and a holistic

review of investment incentives in PJM’s markets in 2026, among other initiatives.

     4. PJM Compliance Filing in Docket No. ER26-1479-000

        PJM’s February 23 Compliance Filing in Docket No. ER26-1479-000 generally

sets forth the relative obligations of project developers seeking to serve co-located load,

and PJM. The proposal defines “Co-Located Generating Facility” as “an existing or

planned Generating Facility that is physically connected to a Co-Located Load,” and

“Co-Located Load” as “a configuration that refers to end-use customer load that is

physically connected to the facilities of an existing or planned Generating Facility on the

Project Developer’s side of the Point of Change in Ownership to the Transmission

Provider’s Transmission System.”18 Importantly, these definitions appear to

accommodate not only new generators, but existing generators seeking to serve co-

located load.

disclosures/2026/20260116-pjm-board-letter-re-results-of-the-cifp-process-large-load-additions.pdf.
18

         Additionally, the February 23 Compliance Filing in Docket No. ER26-1479-000

proposes tariff revisions requiring that “[a] Project Developer whose planned

modifications include Co-Located Load configuration shall be required to enter into a

Necessary Studies Agreement with Transmission Provider in the form set forth in Tariff,

Part IX, Subpart G.”19 The proposed tariff revisions would require a Project Developer to

provide the Transmission Provider with “the amount of reduction to Capacity

Interconnection Rights to facilitate the Co-Located Load configuration.”20 The proposed

revisions also provide that:

        Project Developer shall be responsible for the costs of any modifications or
        Network Upgrades identified by Transmission Provider, as applicable, as a
        result of the change to the Interconnection Service Agreement or
        Generation Interconnection Agreement to serve Co-Located Load,
        including to reflect any reduction in Capacity Interconnection Rights.21

“Capacity Interconnection Rights” (“CIRs”) are previously defined in PJM’s tariff as “the

rights to input generation as a Generation Capacity Resource into the Transmission

System at the Point of Interconnection where the generating facilities connect to the

Transmission System.”22 Thus, the proposed revisions appear to accommodate new

generators seeking to serve co-located load, as well as existing generators seeking to

serve co-located load by reducing their CIRs, and, thus, their ability to input generation

onto PJM’s transmission system.

      5. PJM’s Initial Brief

        PJM’s Initial Brief proposes non-rate terms and conditions for the new

transmission services required by the Show Cause Order (Interim NITS and the two

Contract Demand Transmission Services). PJM states that Interim NITS “will

significantly affect the PJM Load Forecast and expected demand.”23 PJM seeks an

effective date of June 1, 2029, for tariff revisions implementing the three new

transmission services. In support of this effective date, PJM explains that it is unlikely

that generation intended to serve Co-Located Load will be constructed and operational

before June 1, 2029, which suggests that PJM does not intend for existing load to be

eligible for these Co-Located Load transmission services.24



                                        PROTEST

        As explained by the Commission in the Show Cause Order, PJM’s tariff is unjust

and unreasonable because it does not contain provisions addressing with sufficient clarity

or consistency the rates, terms, and conditions of service that apply to generators serving

Co-Located Load and Eligible Customers taking transmission service on behalf of Co-

Located Load.25 However, in light of the recent issuance of Statement of Principles issued

jointly by the White House and thirteen governors of states within PJM, the Ratepayer

Protection Pledge, and PJM’s proposed Reliability Backstop Procurement applicable to




23
   PJM Initial Brief at 79.
24
   PJM Initial Brief at 79.
25
   See Show Cause Order at P 2.


                                              8
 new capacity resources, PJM’s proposed terms and conditions remain without sufficient

clarity and consistency.

        The Statement of Principles directed PJM to hold a reliability backstop auction to

procure new capacity resources, which PJM has proposed to implement in two phases—

the first in September 2026 and the second in March 2027.26 The Statement of Principles

further urges that costs of such new capacity should go primarily to load serving entities

with new data centers that have not self-procured new capacity or agreed to be

curtailable.27 The Ratepayer Protection Pledge also commits the major data center

developers to procure new capacity resources to serve their needs. Thus, the thrust of the

Statement of Principles and the Ratepayer Protection Pledge is that generally new data

centers should pay for new capacity.

        Under this framework, new data centers that are not served by self-procured new

co-located generation could be subject to higher costs from the load serving entity as

result of the reliability backstop auction. But PJM’s proposed terms and conditions do not

explain how existing capacity resources that shift to co-located arrangements with new

data centers would be treated relative to the PJM’s proposed RBP. For example, it is

unclear whether capacity from existing generators that remove themselves from the

capacity market and enter co-location arrangements with new data center load would

need to be replaced with new capacity through the RBP or in the regular BRA to serve

05---pjm-reliability-backstop-procurement-design---pjm-presentation.pdf.
27
   See Statement of Principles at 1.


                                                   9
 existing load. Additionally, it is unclear whether new data center load that co-locates with

an existing generator will be included in the cost allocation of the reliability backstop

procurement.

       If the capacity of existing generation that shifts to serve new co-located data center

load is added to the BRA, ratepayers would be saddled with enormous costs that should

be assigned to the co-located load, in contravention of the Statement of Principles and the

Ratepayer Protection Pledge. For example, analysis by PJM’s Independent Market

Monitor concluded that if 1,000 UCAP MW of nuclear capacity in Maryland was

removed—due to shifting to serving a co-located load for example—total market

revenues for the 2025/2026 BRA would increase by more than $3.6 billion.28 Yet PJM’s

compliance filing provides no explanation as to how such costs would be paid by new co-

located data center load rather than being shifted to existing ratepayers.

       PJM’s proposed terms and conditions thus leave significant and fundamental

questions unanswered with respect to how existing generation can serve new co-located

data center load. Without providing more details regarding how the proposal will align

with PJM’s plans for the RBA, PJM’s proposal remains unclear and inconsistent with the

Statement of Principles underpinning the RBA. This lack of clarity and consistency

causes PJM’s proposed terms and conditions to remain unjust and unreasonable. At a

minimum, the Commission should require PJM’s proposal to be consistent across the co-




28
  See Comments to the Maryland PSC Senate Bill 1 Co-location Study Administrative Docket PC 61
(Sep. 24, 2024) at 3,
https://www.monitoringanalytics.com/filings/2024/IMM_Comments_MDPSC_PC61_20240924.pdf.


                                                10
 location compliance dockets so the effect on ratepayers may be understood and

demonstrate how its proposal meets the ratepayer protection standards set forth in the

Statement of Principles and Ratepayer Protection Pledge.



                                     CONCLUSION

       The issuance of the Statement of Principles by the White House and thirteen

governors of states within PJM calling for an RBA to serve new data center load and the

Ratepayer Protection Pledge are salient intervening events that have occurred since the

Show Cause Order issued. However, despite the significance of PJM’s work toward

implementing an RBP, fundamental issues surrounding how existing generators that shift

to serve Co-Located Load under PJM’s proposed tariff revisions will be treated relative to

the RBP remain unaddressed. As a result, PJM’s proposed revisions do not provide the

clarity and consistency required by the Show Cause Order. PJM’s proposed terms and

conditions thus are unjust and unreasonable without a complete picture of how they will

interact with PJM’s planned RBP. The Commission should clarify how its proposal meets

the ratepayer protection standards set forth in the Statement of Principles and Ratepayer

Protection Pledge and defer action on the proposed revisions until after PJM proposes

tariff revisions to implement its planned RBP.



                                                 Respectfully submitted,

                                                 DAVID S. LAPP
